result.summary: Pausanias gives another version of how Oxylus won Elis, through a single combat between Degmenus and Pyræchmes, and describes his settlement of the land and his family. He then tells how Iphitus revived the Olympic games and sketches Elis's later wars, from Troy to the successors of Alexander.

scenes.title: Oxylus wins Elis by single combat
scenes.summary: Oxylus avoids Elis on the march, then wins the kingdom when his slinger Pyræchmes beats Degmenus. He settles Ætolians among the Epeans and honours Dius and Augeas.
scenes.stakes: Oxylus risks losing the kingdom of Elis, which Dius will not hand over without a contest.

scenes.title: Oxylus's colonists and family
scenes.summary: Following an oracle, Oxylus invites Agorius and some Achæans to settle. His son Ætolus dies and is buried at the gate by oracle, and Laias succeeds him.

scenes.title: Iphitus restores the Olympic games
scenes.summary: Iphitus, with Delphi's advice, revives the games and the truce, and has Elis sacrifice to Hercules. His parentage is disputed.
scenes.stakes: Greece is ruined by civil wars and pestilence, and Iphitus seeks relief from the god.

scenes.title: Elis in later wars
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the wars of Elis, from Troy and the Persian invasion to Sparta, Philip and the Macedonians.
scenes.stakes: Elis's independence is threatened by Sparta and Macedon.

notable_quotes.reason: The oracle's riddle that Ætolus's body lie neither in nor out of the city.

analysis.text: The passage shows how founding stories and oracles explain Elean customs, such as the tomb at the gate and the sacrifices to Augeas.
Iphitus's restoration of the games and the sacred truce reflects the Olympic festival's role in Greek unity, with Elis's later politics shaped by rivalry with Sparta and Macedon.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes that the inscription at Olympia, the Greek tradition and Elean records all gave different fathers for Iphitus.

language_notes.text: The sons of Aristomachus were the Heracleidae (descendants of Hercules) who led the Dorian invasion of the Peloponnese; Oxylus was their Ætolian guide.
"Contention" means a contest or fight; Dius proposes a duel between champions rather than a battle between whole armies.
The Epeans were the older inhabitants of Elis; the Ætolians were settlers from Oxylus's own homeland.
Augeas was a legendary king of Elis, known from the myth of Hercules cleaning his stables; he received hero-cult sacrifices.
Orestes was the son of Agamemnon, so Agorius descends from Pelops through the house of Atreus.
The oracle's riddle is satisfied by burial in the gateway, which is neither inside nor outside the city.
Lycurgus is the traditional Spartan lawgiver; naming him as a contemporary dates Iphitus, whose revival is traditionally placed in the early 8th century BC or earlier.
"Bethought him to ask" means he took it into his mind to consult the oracle; archaic reflexive phrasing.
Hercules was thought hostile because he had earlier made war on Elis and King Augeas, according to the Elean legend.
Refers to the Elean–Spartan war around 400 BC, when King Agis invaded Elis; Pausanias described its settlement in his Laconian book.
"Intestine factions" means internal civil strife within Elis.

context_notes.text: Slingers and bowmen were light-armed fighters; pairing a slinger against an archer makes this a contest of missile weapons.
Delphi was the sanctuary of Apollo, whose oracle often directed colonization and settlement.
The gymnasium was the place for athletic training; its master performing the rite shows the hero-cult continuing in Pausanias's own time.
The Pythian Priestess was the Pythia, the woman who delivered Apollo's oracles at Delphi.
Philip II of Macedon defeated the Greek allies at Chæronea in 338 BC, ending Greek independence.
After Alexander died in 323 BC, Greek states rose against Macedonian rule in the Lamian War, led by Athens, and were defeated by Antipater.

literary_notes.text: The oracle's paradoxical demand sounds impossible, yet it is resolved cleverly by the gate, a boundary space.
Pausanias speaks in the first person, stating his method and limits as a historian by excluding private persons.
Pausanias frames the revival as a response to crisis, giving the games a religious and pacifying purpose.
The phrase "could not keep his hands off Greece" paints Philip as grasping and aggressive.
